title: Israel's neighbours: Aram, Tyre, Moab, Sheba and Ethiopia

intro.text: Israel's neighbours appear in Scripture where they touch Israel and Judah: as allies, payers of tribute, enemies or visitors. This group gathers nine of them: five kings of Aram at Damascus (as the site's person records count them), Hiram of Tyre, Mesha of Moab, and two queens, of Sheba and of the Ethiopians.
The KJV calls Aram “Syria”. Its kings at Damascus appear from Asa's day (1 Kings 15) to Ahaz's, when the king of Assyria took Damascus “and slew Rezin” (2 Kings 16:9).
Scripture gives none of them a regnal formula, a length of reign or a verdict. Each page quotes what Scripture says of them instead, and adds no judgement.

Three pages share the name Ben-hadad, following the site's three person records. Scripture names a Ben-hadad son of Tabrimon, a Ben-hadad of Elisha's day and a Ben-hadad son of Hazael; whether the first two, and the king of 1 Kings 20, are one man or more is shown as a question with its holders.

Records from outside the Bible are kept apart from Scripture: Assyrian annals (in Luckenbill's and Rogers's translations), the Mesha Stele (in Driver's translation, shown beside 2 Kings 3, not blended with it), Tyrian historians as Josephus quotes them, and Greek and Roman writers on the queens of Ethiopia. Dates are reconstructions; where no year is known, the page says so.

rulers.name: Ben-hadad
rulers.title: King of Syria (Aram), who dwelt at Damascus
rulers.tagline: Paid by Asa to break his league with Baasha.

capital.name: Damascus
capital.note: “king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus” (1 Kings 15:18).

identifications.text: The site's person record for this Ben-hadad holds two passages: Ben-hadad son of Tabrimon, whom Asa paid (1 Kings 15:18–20; 2 Chronicles 16:2–4), and the Ben-hadad who besieged Samaria in Ahab's reign (1 Kings 20). Scripture does not say whether they are one man. This page shows each passage on its own and sets out the question with its holders.
He is not the Ben-hadad of Elisha's day (2 Kings 6:24; 8:7) nor Ben-hadad the son of Hazael (2 Kings 13:24); each has his own page.
Jeremiah's oracle on Damascus, “it shall consume the palaces of Ben-hadad”, is held on this record. The verse names no king of its own day; it uses the name of Damascus's palaces.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign for any Ben-hadad.

dates.label: Placed by Scripture's kings of Israel and Judah (Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young)
dates.note: No year of his own is known. His contemporaries in 1 Kings 15 are Asa (912/911–871/870 BC) and Baasha (909/908–886/885 BC). If the Ben-hadad of 1 Kings 20 is the same man, he was still reigning in Ahab's time (874/873–853 BC).

scriptureSays.text: Asa took the silver and gold left in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the palace, and sent them “to Ben-hadad, the son of Tabrimon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus”.
Asa's message: “There is a league between me and thee, and between my father and thy father … come and break thy league with Baasha king of Israel, that he may depart from me.”
“So Ben-hadad hearkened unto king Asa”, and sent his captains against the cities of Israel.
In 1 Kings 20, “Ben-hadad the king of Syria” besieged Samaria with thirty-two kings, was routed there and again at Aphek, and begged for his life; Ahab made a covenant with him and let him go.
A prophet told Ahab that the LORD had appointed this king “to utter destruction”.
Jeremiah, of Damascus: “I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall consume the palaces of Ben-hadad.”

claim.text: Asa delivered the silver and gold “into the hand of his servants” and sent them to Ben-hadad at Damascus.
Asa asked him to “break thy league with Baasha king of Israel”, and “Ben-hadad hearkened unto king Asa”.
His captains “smote Ijon, and Dan, and Abel-beth-maachah, and all Cinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali”.
When Baasha heard of it, “he left off building of Ramah, and dwelt in Tirzah”; Asa carried off its stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah.
With thirty-two kings he besieged Samaria and demanded: “Thy silver and thy gold is mine; thy wives also and thy children, even the goodliest, are mine.”
While “Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk in the pavilions”, the young men of the princes of the provinces came out; the Syrians fled, and he “escaped on an horse with the horsemen”.

events.label: The war moved to the plain

claim.text: His servants advised: “Their gods are gods of the hills … let us fight against them in the plain”, and to put captains in the kings' places. At the return of the year he went up to Aphek.
After seven days facing each other, Israel “slew of the Syrians an hundred thousand footmen in one day”; a wall fell on twenty-seven thousand in Aphek, and Ben-hadad fled into an inner chamber.

His servants came out in sackcloth with ropes on their heads: “Thy servant Ben-hadad saith, I pray thee, let me live.” He offered to restore cities, and Ahab “made a covenant with him, and sent him away”.
“Concerning Damascus … I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall consume the palaces of Ben-hadad.”

worship.text: His servants said of Israel, “Their gods are gods of the hills”; a man of God answered that the LORD would give the Syrians into Ahab's hand, “and ye shall know that I am the LORD”.

alliances.text: A league with Judah: Asa speaks of a league “between me and thee, and between my father and thy father”.
A league with Baasha of Israel, which he broke for Asa's silver and gold.
A covenant with Ahab after Aphek: “thou shalt make streets for thee in Damascus, as my father made in Samaria”.

people.text: His captains struck the north of Israel, “all the land of Naphtali”.

Samaria under siege: he claimed its king's silver, gold, wives and children, then swore: “The gods do so unto me, and more also, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls for all the people that follow me.”

claim.text: Chronicles: Hanani rebuked Asa for relying on the king of Syria rather than on the LORD.

quote.text: Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand

claim.text: Promised Ahab victory over Ben-hadad's “great multitude”, and warned that “at the return of the year the king of Syria will come up against thee”.
Answered the Syrians' saying that the LORD “is God of the hills, but he is not God of the valleys” with a promise of victory.

person.name: One of the sons of the prophets

claim.text: Condemned Ahab for letting Ben-hadad go.

quote.text: Because thou hast let go out of thy hand a man whom I appointed to utter destruction, therefore thy life shall go for his life

claim.text: In his oracle on Damascus, named its palaces after Ben-hadad.

quote.text: it shall consume the palaces of Ben-hadad

claim.text: Asa bought his help against Baasha with the temple's and the palace's silver and gold.
Baasha had a league with him and lost northern cities when he broke it; in 1 Kings 20 the Ben-hadad of this record fights Ahab.

outside.name: Monolith Inscription of Shalmaneser III, from Kurkh

claim.text: At Karkar, Shalmaneser fought “Hadad-ezer, of Aram (? Damascus)” with 1,200 chariots, 1,200 cavalry and 20,000 soldiers, beside “Ahab, the Israelite”. The inscription names no Ben-hadad; who this Hadad-ezer is in Scripture's terms is a question below.

outside.name: Nicolaus of Damascus, quoted by Josephus
outside.date: Nicolaus wrote in the 1st century BC; Josephus about AD 93

claim.text: Josephus quotes Nicolaus: after a king Hadad who fought David, “his posterity reigned for ten generations, each of his successors receiving from his father that his dominion, and this his name”, and “the third” laid waste Samaria. Josephus adds: “this is that Hadad who made the expedition against Samaria, in the reign of Ahab”.

first.text: Kings: Asa sent “all the silver and the gold that were left”; the captains struck Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maachah, “all Cinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali”. No year is given.

second.text: Chronicles: “In the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa”; the captains struck Ijon, Dan, “Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali”.

first.text: Kings tells the alliance without comment.

second.text: Chronicles adds the seer Hanani's rebuke: “therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand … from henceforth thou shalt have wars.”

questions.question: Is the Ben-hadad of Asa's day (1 Kings 15) the same man as Ahab's enemy (1 Kings 20)?

views.label: Two men: Asa's Ben-hadad and his son
views.holders: C. F. Keil (tr. 1872), pp. 221, 261 and 266–267; T. Nicol, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Keil counts three kings of Damascus called Ben-hadad: the son of Tabrimon, “his son in the time of Ahab”, and the son of Hazael. He reads the cities taken by Ahab's enemy's father (1 Kings 20:34) as a war with Omri “of which no account has been preserved”. Nicol calls Ahab's opponent Benhadad II, “in all probability the son of Benhadad I”.

views.label: A name handed down in one line of kings
views.holders: Nicolaus of Damascus (1st century BC), quoted by Josephus, Antiquities 7.5.2 (about AD 93)

argument.text: Nicolaus says each of Hadad's successors received “his dominion, and this his name”, for ten generations; Josephus takes the third of them to be the king who besieged Samaria under Ahab.

views.label: Scripture leaves it open
views.holders: Our reading of the text

argument.text: 1 Kings 20 never gives Ahab's enemy a father's name. He speaks of cities “which my father took from thy father” and streets his father made in Samaria, while 1 Kings 15 tells only of cities taken from Baasha in Naphtali.

questions.question: Is Ahab's Ben-hadad the king the Assyrian records call “Hadad-ezer” (or “Bir-idri”)?

views.label: Yes: the name is to be read Bir-idri, that is Ben-hadad
views.holders: R. W. Rogers (1912), p. 296, note 1, after Delitzsch and Winckler; T. Nicol, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Rogers reads the Assyrian name “Bir-idri” and writes: “He is the king who is called Benhadad in 1 Kings 20”, 2 Kings 6:24 and 8:7–15. Nicol calls Benhadad II “the Hadad-ezer, or Hadad-'idri, of the monuments”.

views.label: The Assyrian name is read Hadad-ezer (Adad-idri)
views.holders: D. D. Luckenbill (1926), §611; Schrader, Zimmern and Ungnad, as reported by Rogers (1912)

argument.text: Luckenbill translates the name “Hadad-ezer”; Rogers reports that Schrader, Zimmern and Ungnad read it “Adad-idri or Hadad-idri”, and that Zimmern later changed his mind. This is a question of how to read the name: the sources used here do not say whether these scholars took Hadad-ezer to be a different king from Scripture's Ben-hadad.

questions.question: Was Hezion, Ben-hadad's grandfather, the Rezon who “reigned in Damascus” in Solomon's day (1 Kings 11:24)?

views.label: Possibly
views.holders: T. Nicol, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Nicol: Hezion “has been with some plausibility identified with Rezon”, the founder of the kingdom of Damascus.

views.label: Not shown even to be probable

argument.text: Keil holds that Tabrimon had been king, but that Hezion's being king and the same man as Rezon “cannot be shown to be even probable”.

notSaid: Scripture gives this Ben-hadad no length of reign, no age, and no account of his death.
1 Kings 15 does not say what Ben-hadad's league with Baasha was, or when it was made.
1 Kings 20 never names the father of the Ben-hadad who besieged Samaria.
Scripture tells of no war between Omri and Damascus, though Ahab's enemy speaks of cities his father took from Ahab's father (1 Kings 20:34).
Scripture does not call Hezion a king, nor say that he is the Rezon of 1 Kings 11.
No Assyrian record used here names a Ben-hadad in Ahab's time; the Monolith names Hadad-ezer.
The “king of Syria” whose captains fought Ahab at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:31) is not named; that he is this Ben-hadad is a reading, and 1 Kings 22 is not on this page.

places.name: Cinneroth
places.note: “All Cinneroth”; the Atlas pin is the lake of Chinnereth

rulers.name: Ben-hadad
otherNames: Ben-hadad king of Syria (in Elisha's day)
rulers.title: King of Syria (Aram) in the days of Elisha
rulers.tagline: Besieged Samaria; smothered on his sickbed.

capital.name: Damascus
capital.note: Elisha came to Damascus when the king was sick (2 Kings 8:7).

identifications.text: This page follows the site's record for the Ben-hadad named in 2 Kings 6:24 and 8:7–9. The unnamed “king of Syria” of 2 Kings 5:1–6:23 (Naaman's master, the hunt for Elisha at Dothan) is left off this page: the text does not name him, and the site's record does not include him.
Whether he is the Ben-hadad of 1 Kings 20 is a question with views below; whether that king is the Hadad-ezer of Shalmaneser III's records is set out on the page of Asa's Ben-hadad.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign; it tells how it ended (2 Kings 8:15).

dates.label: Placed by the Assyrian records and Scripture
dates.note: No year of his own is known. The siege story names no king of Israel; the chapters around it are set in the reign of Joram son of Ahab (852–841 BC on Thiele, McFall and Young). Hazael, who took his throne, was already king of Damascus when Shalmaneser III fought him in his eighteenth year (841 BC).

scriptureSays.text: “Ben-hadad king of Syria gathered all his host, and went up, and besieged Samaria.”
The siege brought a famine in which “an ass’s head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver”.
“The Lord had made the host of the Syrians to hear a noise of chariots, and a noise of horses”, and they fled, leaving their camp.
Sick at Damascus, he sent Hazael to Elisha: “Shall I recover of this disease?”
Hazael called him “Thy son Ben-hadad king of Syria” before the prophet.
“On the morrow, that he took a thick cloth, and dipped it in water, and spread it on his face, so that he died: and Hazael reigned in his stead.”

claim.text: He gathered all his host and besieged Samaria; “there was a great famine in Samaria”.
A woman cried to the king of Israel on the wall: her neighbour had agreed that they would eat their sons, and “we boiled my son, and did eat him”.
Elisha: “To morrow about this time shall a measure of fine flour be sold for a shekel … in the gate of Samaria.”
Hearing “the noise of a great host”, the Syrians said the king of Israel had hired “the kings of the Hittites, and the kings of the Egyptians”, and fled; four lepers found the camp empty.
The scouts followed them to the Jordan: “all the way was full of garments and vessels, which the Syrians had cast away in their haste”.
“Ben-hadad the king of Syria was sick”; he sent Hazael with “forty camels’ burden” of gifts to ask Elisha whether he would recover.
Hazael told him he would recover; the next day the wet cloth was spread on his face, “so that he died: and Hazael reigned in his stead”.

worship.text: He asked through Hazael for a word from Israel's God: “enquire of the LORD by him, saying, Shall I recover of this disease?”

people.text: Samaria's famine under his siege: the king of Israel “had sackcloth within upon his flesh”.
Plenty after his flight: “a measure of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD”.

claim.text: Foretold the end of the famine in besieged Samaria, and told Hazael that his master would die and that Hazael would be king.

quote.text: Go, say unto him, Thou mayest certainly recover: howbeit the LORD hath shewed me that he shall surely die

claim.text: The story calls him only “the king of Israel”, and Elisha calls him “this son of a murderer”. The chapters around it are set in the reign of Joram son of Ahab.
“Hazael reigned in his stead.”

outside.name: Shalmaneser III's records (Black Obelisk; annals from Calah)

claim.text: In his eleventh and fourteenth years Shalmaneser fought “Hadad-ezer of Aram (? Damascus)” and twelve kings; in his eighteenth year (841 BC) his enemy at Damascus is “Hazael of Aram”.

outside.name: Shalmaneser III's statue inscription, from Assur

claim.text: “Hadad-ezer died. Hazael, the son of a nobody, seized the throne” (Luckenbill, 1926). Rogers (1912) translates the same line “Bir-idri forsook his land” and explains it as abdication.

twoAccounts.topic: How the king before Hazael left the throne

first.text: Scripture: on the day after Elisha's answer a thick cloth was dipped in water and spread on Ben-hadad's face, “so that he died: and Hazael reigned in his stead”.

second.text: Shalmaneser's statue inscription: “Hadad-ezer died. Hazael, the son of a nobody, seized the throne” (Luckenbill); “Bir-idri forsook his land” (Rogers). It says nothing of how he died, if he died.

questions.question: Who spread the wet cloth on Ben-hadad's face (2 Kings 8:15)? The verse says only “he”.

views.label: Hazael
views.holders: Josephus, Antiquities 9.4.6 (about AD 93); C. F. Keil (tr. 1872), p. 336; the Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott's Commentary

argument.text: Josephus writes that Hazael “spread a wet cloth, in the nature of a net, over him, and strangled him”. Keil, the Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott take Hazael as the subject, as of the verbs in the verse before.

views.label: Ben-hadad himself, by accident
views.holders: Luther, Schultz, Geddes and Boothroyd, as reported by the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: These commentators supposed Ben-hadad laid the wet cloth on his own face to cool himself and was suffocated; the Pulpit Commentary calls this “very unlikely”.

views.label: A servant
views.holders: H. Ewald, History of Israel, as reported by the Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott

argument.text: Ewald introduced a bath-servant as the one who killed the king; both commentaries reject it, noting that Hazael is named at the end of the verse as the new king.

questions.question: Did Elisha say “Thou mayest certainly recover” (the KJV), or “Thou wilt not live” (the written Hebrew, as Keil translates it), in 2 Kings 8:10?

views.label: “Thou wilt live” (the Hebrew margin, followed by the KJV)
views.holders: Most commentators, the ancient versions and the Masoretes, as reported by Keil (tr. 1872), p. 334

argument.text: Keil reports that most follow the margin's reading, so that Elisha tells Hazael to say the king will recover, though the LORD has shown he will die.
Keil prefers the written Hebrew, so that Elisha's answer was that the king would not live, and Hazael's report of recovery (verse 14) was his own lie.

questions.question: Is Elisha's Ben-hadad the same king who fought Ahab in 1 Kings 20?

views.label: Yes, one king (Ben-hadad II)
views.holders: R. W. Rogers (1912), p. 296, note 1; T. Nicol, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Rogers identifies the Assyrians' Bir-idri with the Ben-hadad of 1 Kings 20, 2 Kings 6:24 and 8:7–15; Nicol's Benhadad II both fights Ahab and is murdered by Hazael.

views.label: Scripture leaves it open
views.holders: Our reading of the text

argument.text: Kings never says whether Ahab's enemy lived on into Elisha's time; between the two stories come Ahab's death and the reign of Ahaziah. The site's person data files 1 Kings 20 under Asa's Ben-hadad and gives this one only 2 Kings 6:24 and 8:7–9.

notSaid: Scripture never gives this Ben-hadad's father, his age, or the length of his reign.
2 Kings 5–6 speaks of “the king of Syria” without naming him; that he is this Ben-hadad is a reading, not a statement.
Scripture does not name the king of Israel during the siege of Samaria.
The Assyrian records used here never name a Ben-hadad; they name Hadad-ezer (or Bir-idri) and then Hazael.

places.name: Damascus
places.note: Where he lay sick and died

rulers.name: Hazael
rulers.title: King of Syria (Aram) at Damascus
rulers.tagline: Elisha wept over the evil he would do to Israel.

capital.name: Damascus
capital.note: Shalmaneser III calls Damascus “his royal city”.

identifications.text: The Hazael of 1 Kings 19 and 2 Kings 8–13. Amos's “house of Hazael” names his line.

Published summaries of the editors' reports say that A. Biran and J. Naveh (1995) credit the Aramaic stele from Tel Dan to Hazael, and that the king's name does not survive on the fragments found; the editors' articles themselves were not read for this page.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign; he oppressed Israel “all the days of Jehoahaz” (2 Kings 13:22).

dates.label: From Shalmaneser III's records and Scripture, on the main system's dates
dates.note: Already king of Damascus in Shalmaneser III's eighteenth year (841 BC); in his fourteenth year (845 BC) the king of Damascus was still Hadad-ezer. His death is not dated by any record used here: Scripture puts it after he had oppressed Israel “all the days of Jehoahaz”, who died in 798 BC on Thiele, McFall and Young's dates.

scriptureSays.text: At Horeb the LORD told Elijah: “anoint Hazael to be king over Syria”.
“Him that escapeth the sword of Hazael shall Jehu slay.”

Elisha wept and told him: “I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel: their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child.”
Hazael answered: “is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?” Elisha: “The LORD hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria.”
“In those days the LORD began to cut Israel short: and Hazael smote them in all the coasts of Israel.”
The LORD “delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael, all their days”.
“So Hazael king of Syria died; and Ben-hadad his son reigned in his stead.”

claim.text: The LORD sent Elijah to the wilderness of Damascus to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu king over Israel, and Elisha prophet in his room.
Ben-hadad, sick, sent him to Elisha with “every good thing of Damascus, forty camels’ burden”.
Elisha “settled his countenance stedfastly, until he was ashamed: and the man of God wept”, and told him he would be king.
He told his master he would recover; the next day the wet cloth was spread on the king's face, “and Hazael reigned in his stead”.
Joram of Israel, with Ahaziah of Judah, went “to the war against Hazael king of Syria in Ramoth-gilead”; the Syrians wounded Joram.
“Joram had kept Ramoth-gilead, he and all Israel, because of Hazael king of Syria.”

events.label: Israel cut short east of the Jordan

claim.text: He struck “all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the river Arnon, even Gilead and Bashan”.
“Hazael king of Syria went up, and fought against Gath, and took it.”
He “set his face to go up to Jerusalem”; Jehoash of Judah sent him the hallowed things and the gold of the temple and palace, “and he went away from Jerusalem”.
The king of Syria left Jehoahaz only “fifty horsemen, and ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen”, having “made them like the dust by threshing”.
“So Hazael king of Syria died; and Ben-hadad his son reigned in his stead.”

worship.text: To buy him off, Jehoash of Judah gave up the hallowed things that Jehoshaphat, Jehoram and Ahaziah had dedicated, his own hallowed things, and the gold of the house of the LORD.

alliances.text: Tribute from Judah: Jehoash sent it all “to Hazael king of Syria: and he went away from Jerusalem”.

people.text: He took from Israel the land east of the Jordan: Gilead, Gad, Reuben and Manasseh, as far as the Arnon, Gilead and Bashan.
“Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.”
Jehoahaz “besought the LORD”, and “the LORD gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians”.
Amos: “they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron”.

claim.text: Was sent to anoint Hazael king over Syria.

quote.text: anoint Hazael to be king over Syria

claim.text: Wept before Hazael at Damascus and foretold his kingship and his cruelty to Israel.

quote.text: The LORD hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria

claim.text: Foretold fire on “the house of Hazael” for threshing Gilead.

quote.text: I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, which shall devour the palaces of Ben-hadad

claim.text: He fought Joram at Ramoth-gilead, cut Israel short in Jehu's days, and oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.
Ahaziah went with Joram against him; Jehoash paid him to turn back from Jerusalem.
Shalmaneser fought Hazael in his eighteenth year (841 BC) and again in his twenty-first, when he took “four of his cities”.

outside.name: Shalmaneser III's annals (Black Obelisk and Calah annals)

claim.text: “Hazael of Aram (Syria) trusted in the masses of his troops”, made Mount Saniru, “in front of Mount Lebanon”, his stronghold, and was defeated; Shalmaneser lists 16,000 of his warriors slain and 1,131 chariots taken (the Black Obelisk says 1,121). In the twenty-first year he “captured” four of Hazael's cities.

outside.name: Shalmaneser III's statue inscription, from Assur

claim.text: “Hazael, the son of a nobody, seized the throne”, gathered his army, was defeated, and fled; Shalmaneser advanced “as far as Damascus, his royal city”. The line before reads “Hadad-ezer died” (Luckenbill) or “Bir-idri forsook his land” (Rogers).

An Aramaic inscription whose speaker, a king of Aram, claims to have killed a king of Israel and a king of the house of David. Published summaries report that Biran and Naveh restore the names as Joram son of Ahab and Ahaziah son of Jehoram. Described here in our own words from those summaries: the editors' articles were not read, and there is no public-domain translation.

outside.name: Josephus on the kings of Damascus in his own day

claim.text: Josephus writes that Ben-hadad and Hazael “are honored to this day as gods” by the people of Damascus, “by reason of their benefactions, and their building them temples”.

first.text: Kings: Hazael took Gath and turned toward Jerusalem; Jehoash sent him the hallowed things and the gold, “and he went away from Jerusalem”.

second.text: Chronicles names no king: “the host of Syria came up against him”, destroyed “all the princes of the people”, sent the spoil “unto the king of Damascus”, and “executed judgment against Joash”.

twoAccounts.topic: Who killed Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah

first.text: Kings: Jehu shot Joram “between his arms”, and had Ahaziah smitten as he fled.

second.text: The Tel Dan stele, as published summaries describe it (the editors' articles were not read): its Aramaean speaker claims to have killed a king of Israel and a king of the house of David, names its editors restore. Neither record is used here to correct the other.

questions.question: Was Hazael ever anointed? The LORD told Elijah to do it (1 Kings 19:15); Scripture records no anointing.

views.label: Not literally: he was told he would be king

argument.text: Keil holds that only Jehu was really anointed; “Hazael was merely told by Elisha that he would be king” (2 Kings 8:13), so the word is used figuratively here.

views.label: Anointed in secret by Elijah, then again by Elisha
views.holders: Earlier interpreters, as reported (and rejected) by Keil (tr. 1872), p. 260

argument.text: Keil reports the opinion that Elijah anointed Hazael and Jehu at once but kept it secret, and that Elisha repeated it when their time came; he finds it ruled out by the account of Jehu's anointing in 2 Kings 9.

notSaid: Scripture records the command to anoint Hazael (1 Kings 19:15) but no anointing.
Scripture does not name Hazael's father; Shalmaneser's inscription calls him “the son of a nobody”.
Scripture gives him no length of reign and no burial.
Scripture says nothing of his wars with Assyria.
Chronicles tells of a Syrian army in Joash's day without naming Hazael (2 Chronicles 24:23–24).

places.name: Aroer
places.note: “which is by the river Arnon”, the southern edge of his conquest

rulers.name: Ben-hadad
rulers.title: King of Syria (Aram), son of Hazael
rulers.tagline: Three times beaten by Jehoash of Israel.

identifications.text: Ben-hadad the son of Hazael (2 Kings 13:3, 24–25); not the earlier Ben-hadads of Asa's and Elisha's days.
T. Nicol (ISBE, 1915) identifies him with “Mari’”, the king of Damascus in Adad-nirari III's inscriptions, and says this “is now generally believed”; Mari’ “means in Aramaic ‘lord’”.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign.

dates.label: From Scripture, on the main system's dates
dates.note: He followed Hazael, who oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz (died 798 BC on Thiele, McFall and Young); Jehoash of Israel (798–782 BC) beat him three times. When his reign ended is not known.

scriptureSays.text: The LORD delivered Israel “into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael, all their days”.
“So Hazael king of Syria died; and Ben-hadad his son reigned in his stead.”
“Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again out of the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael the cities, which he had taken out of the hand of Jehoahaz his father by war. Three times did Joash beat him.”
Amos: “I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, which shall devour the palaces of Ben-hadad.”

claim.text: Israel was given into the hand of Hazael “and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael”.

The dying Elisha had Joash shoot eastward: “The arrow of the LORD’s deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria”; because Joash struck the ground only three times, “thou shalt smite Syria but thrice”.
“Ben-hadad his son reigned in his stead.”
“Three times did Joash beat him, and recovered the cities of Israel.”

people.text: Israel's cities taken in Jehoahaz's days were recovered from him by Jehoash.
“The children of Israel dwelt in their tents, as beforetime.”

claim.text: On his deathbed foretold three victories over Syria.

quote.text: thou shalt smite Syria but thrice

claim.text: Foretold fire on the house of Hazael and the palaces of Ben-hadad.

quote.text: which shall devour the palaces of Ben-hadad

claim.text: He shared his father's oppression of Jehoahaz's Israel and lost its cities to Jehoash.
Adad-nirari III says he shut up “Mari’, king of Aram” in Damascus and received his tribute.

outside.name: Adad-nirari III's inscriptions (Saba’a stele; Nimrud slab)
outside.date: Adad-nirari III's reign; the stele speaks of his fifth year

claim.text: “Against Aram (Syria) I marched, Mari’, king of Aram, — in Damascus, his royal city, I shut him up”; the king became his vassal and paid “2,300 talents of silver, 20 talents of gold, 3,000 talents of copper, 5,000 talents of iron”, garments, “an ivory bed, an ivory couch”. The records do not name a Ben-hadad.
Josephus calls Hazael's son “Adad” and says Joash beat him “in three battles”.

questions.question: Who was the “saviour” who freed Israel from the Syrians (2 Kings 13:5)?

views.label: Adad-nirari III of Assyria
views.holders: T. Nicol, ISBE (1915), “Benhadad” and “Hazael”

argument.text: Nicol takes the saviour to be the Assyrian king whose capture of Damascus crippled Syria, so that Jehoash could recover Israel's cities.

Keil finds the saviour in Jehoahaz's two successors: Jehoash, who took back the cities, and Jeroboam, who restored Israel's borders. He reports and rejects other answers: an angel, Elisha, one of Joash's captains, and Jeroboam alone (Thenius).

questions.question: Did Ben-hadad oppress Israel as king, or under his father?

argument.text: Keil reads 2 Kings 13:3 as falling within Hazael's reign: Ben-hadad oppressed Israel “not as king, but as commander-in-chief under his father”, and “is not even called king in ver. 3”.

views.label: Through both reigns
views.holders: O. Thenius, as reported by Keil (tr. 1872), p. 375

argument.text: Thenius took “all their days” to mean the reigns of Hazael and Ben-hadad; Keil answers that verses 24–25 rule this out.

notSaid: Scripture gives no length of reign and does not tell how his reign ended.
Scripture does not name Adad-nirari III or any “Mari’”; the identification is a modern one.
Kings says Jeroboam son of Joash later “recovered Damascus” (2 Kings 14:28) but names no king of Damascus.

rulers.name: Rezin
rulers.title: King of Syria (Aram) at Damascus
rulers.tagline: With Pekah against Ahaz; slain when Assyria took Damascus.

identifications.text: Rezin king of Syria in the days of Ahaz; not the Rezin whose “children” were among the Nethinim who returned from exile (Ezra 2:48; Nehemiah 7:50).

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign; it tells how it ended (2 Kings 16:9).

dates.label: From the Assyrian records: king by about 738 BC
dates.note: His accession is not dated. He is named in Tiglath-pileser III's tribute list beside Menahem of Samaria, whose tribute Mack (1915) dates to 738 BC; the Assyrian eponym list sends the army “against Damascus” in 733 and 732 BC, and Kings says the king of Assyria took Damascus and slew Rezin.

scriptureSays.text: “In those days the LORD began to send against Judah Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah.”
With Pekah he besieged Ahaz in Jerusalem, “but could not overcome him”.
“Rezin king of Syria recovered Elath to Syria, and drave the Jews from Elath.”
Isaiah to Ahaz: “fear not … for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah”.
“For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin.”
“The king of Assyria went up against Damascus, and took it, and carried the people of it captive to Kir, and slew Rezin.”

claim.text: In the closing lines of Jotham's reign Kings says that “the LORD began to send against Judah Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah”.
“Syria is confederate with Ephraim”; they planned to “set a king in the midst of it, even the son of Tabeal”.
Rezin and Pekah “came up to Jerusalem to war: and they besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him”.
He “drave the Jews from Elath”, and “the Syrians came to Elath, and dwelt there unto this day”.
Ahaz sent to Tiglath-pileser: “save me out of the hand of the king of Syria”, with the silver and gold of the temple and the palace.
The king of Assyria took Damascus, carried its people to Kir, “and slew Rezin”.

worship.text: Chronicles: after his defeat Ahaz “sacrificed unto the gods of Damascus, which smote him”.

alliances.text: Alliance with Pekah of Israel against Ahaz: “Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have taken evil counsel against thee”.
Their plan: a king of their own choosing in Judah, “the son of Tabeal”.

people.text: When the alliance was reported, Ahaz's heart “was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind”.
He drove the Jews from Elath.
Chronicles: the king of Syria carried “a great multitude” of Judah captive to Damascus.

claim.text: Told Ahaz that the plan of Rezin and Pekah “shall not stand”, and that the riches of Damascus would be carried off by the king of Assyria.

quote.text: For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin

claim.text: His ally against Judah.
Besieged by Rezin and Pekah, Ahaz called himself the Assyrian king's “servant” and “son”.
The king of Assyria “hearkened unto” Ahaz, took Damascus and slew Rezin.

outside.name: Tiglath-pileser III's tribute lists
outside.date: Undated in the annals; Mack (1915) put Menahem's tribute in 738 BC

claim.text: Among the kings who paid tribute: “Rasunnu (Rezin) of Aram, Menihimmu (Menahem) of Samerina (Samaria), Hirummu (Hiram) of Tyre”. Luckenbill notes that the order of the annal fragments is uncertain.

outside.name: Tiglath-pileser III's annals: the war on Aram

claim.text: A broken passage tells of a king, whose name is lost, shut up “like a bird in a cage” in his city while his gardens were cut down; then: “Hadaru, the father’s house of Resin of Aram (Syria), [where] he was born, I besieged, I captured”, and “591 cities of 16 districts of Aram (Syria), I destroyed”.
The year-names for 733 and 732 BC both record a campaign against Damascus.
Nicol reports, after Schrader, that a tablet recording Rezin's death was found and read by Sir Henry Rawlinson and then lost.

first.text: Kings: Rezin and Pekah besieged Ahaz, “but could not overcome him”.

second.text: Chronicles: “the LORD his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Syria; and they smote him, and carried away a great multitude of them captives, and brought them to Damascus.”

first.text: Kings: the king of Assyria “hearkened unto him”, took Damascus and slew Rezin.

second.text: Chronicles: “Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria came unto him, and distressed him, but strengthened him not.”

questions.question: Did Rezin take Elath for Syria, or give it back to Edom (2 Kings 16:6)?

views.label: For Syria, as the text is written
views.holders: Josephus, Antiquities 9.12.1 (about AD 93); C. F. Keil (tr. 1872), pp. 402–403; J. R. Lumby (1887)

argument.text: Josephus says Rezin took Elath and “peopled it with Syrians”. Keil and Lumby keep the written text: the Edomites already lived in their own land and could not be said to come to Elath.

views.label: To Edom
views.holders: T. Nicol, ISBE (1915); Ellicott's Commentary

argument.text: “Syria” and “Edom” look alike in Hebrew writing. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew margin, many manuscripts, the Greek and the Latin read “Edomites”; Nicol writes that “it is agreed” to read Edom.

views.label: Both: Syria took it, Edom returned
views.holders: David Kimchi, as reported by John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Kimchi explains that the word is written “Syrians” because the king of Syria took the city, and read “Edomites” because by his means the Edomites returned to it.

notSaid: Scripture does not name Rezin's father or say how he came to the throne.
Scripture gives no length of reign; it says only that the king of Assyria “slew Rezin” (2 Kings 16:9), not how.
Isaiah's “burden of Damascus” (Isaiah 17:1–3) does not name him.
No Assyrian text used here describes his death; the tablet said to record it is lost.

rulers.name: Hiram
rulers.title: King of Tyre
rulers.tagline: Cedar for David's house and for Solomon's temple.

identifications.text: Hiram king of Tyre, called Huram in Chronicles. Not Hiram the craftsman, “a widow’s son of the tribe of Naphtali”, whom Solomon fetched out of Tyre to cast the temple's brass (1 Kings 7:13–14); he has his own page.
Not the “Hirummu (Hiram) of Tyre” who paid tribute to Tiglath-pileser III beside Menahem of Samaria, more than two centuries later.
The page treats the Hiram of David's day and of Solomon's as one king, as Scripture's “Hiram was ever a lover of David” suggests; the question is shown with its holders.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign; Josephus, quoting Menander, gives thirty-four years.

dates.label: Our own count, from Josephus's Tyrian figures and the main system's date for the temple
dates.note: Our own count, shown so it can be checked: Josephus puts the founding of the temple in Hiram's twelfth year (Against Apion 1.18; the eleventh in Antiquities 8.3.1) and gives him thirty-four years (Menander). The temple was begun in Solomon's fourth year (1 Kings 6:1), 967 BC on Young's dating. If 967 BC was Hiram's twelfth year, his first was 978 BC (967 + 11), and thirty-four years run to 945 BC (978 − 33): about 978–945 BC. On the “eleventh year” figure every date moves one year later, to about 977–944 BC. Keil holds that the temple date is Josephus's own reckoning rather than Menander's, and that Hiram may have reigned longer, since Scripture makes him David's friend too.

scriptureSays.text: “Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, and carpenters, and masons: and they built David an house.”
He sent his servants to Solomon at his anointing, “for Hiram was ever a lover of David”.
Hearing Solomon's request he said: “Blessed be the LORD this day, which hath given unto David a wise son over this great people.”
“There was peace between Hiram and Solomon; and they two made a league together.”
Of the twenty cities Solomon gave him: “What cities are these which thou hast given me, my brother?”
Chronicles' Huram, writing to Solomon: “Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, that made heaven and earth.”

claim.text: He sent cedar trees, carpenters and masons, “and they built David an house”.
He sent his servants to Solomon, “for he had heard that they had anointed him king in the room of his father”.

events.label: Cedar and fir for the temple

claim.text: Solomon asked for cedars hewn out of Lebanon; Hiram answered, “I will do all thy desire concerning timber of cedar, and concerning timber of fir.”
Hiram promised that his servants would bring the timber down from Lebanon to the sea and float it to the place Solomon named; in Chronicles the promise names the port, Joppa.
“Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand measures of wheat for food to his household, and twenty measures of pure oil: thus gave Solomon to Hiram year by year.”
“They two made a league together.”
“Solomon’s builders and Hiram’s builders did hew them, and the stonesquarers: so they prepared timber and stones to build the house.”
When the two houses were finished, Solomon gave him twenty cities in Galilee; “they pleased him not”, and he called them “the land of Cabul”.
“And Hiram sent to the king sixscore talents of gold.”

events.label: Seamen for the Red Sea fleet

claim.text: He sent “shipmen that had knowledge of the sea” with Solomon's servants from Ezion-geber to Ophir; they brought back 420 talents of gold.
“The navy also of Hiram, that brought gold from Ophir, brought in from Ophir great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones”, used for pillars and for harps.
“The king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram”, coming once in three years with gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks.

worship.text: He blessed Israel's God: “Blessed be the LORD this day, which hath given unto David a wise son.”
Chronicles: “Because the LORD hath loved his people, he hath made thee king over them.”

building.text: Cedar, carpenters and masons for David's house.
Cedar and fir from Lebanon for Solomon's temple and house, and his builders working beside Solomon's.

alliances.text: A league with Solomon, paid in wheat and oil “year by year”.
Twenty cities of Galilee, which did not please him.
Joint fleets to Ophir and with the navy of Tharshish.

people.text: Solomon's levy of thirty thousand men worked in Lebanon “ten thousand a month by courses”.
Solomon asked for Hiram's hewers, “for thou knowest that there is not among us any that can skill to hew timber like unto the Sidonians”.

claim.text: He built David's house and was Solomon's partner in building and at sea.

outside.name: Menander of Ephesus, quoted by Josephus

claim.text: “When Abibalus was dead, his son Hiram received the kingdom from him, who, when he had lived fifty-three years, reigned thirty-four.” Menander says he cut timber on Libanus for the roofs of temples and built temples of Hercules and Astarte, and that under him Abdemon, “a very youth in age”, “always conquered the difficult problems which Solomon, king of Jerusalem, commanded him to explain” (Antiquities 8.5.3).

Dius says that Solomon sent riddles to Hiram on terms that whoever could not solve them would pay; Hiram paid, but afterwards solved them “by means of Abdemon, a man of Tyre”, set riddles of his own that Solomon could not solve, and won the money back.
Josephus dates the temple to the twelfth year of Hiram's reign, 143 years and eight months before Carthage was founded (Against Apion 1.18); in the Antiquities (8.3.1) he says the eleventh year.

first.text: Kings: “twenty thousand measures of wheat for food to his household, and twenty measures of pure oil”, year by year.

second.text: Chronicles: for the hewers, “twenty thousand measures of beaten wheat, and twenty thousand measures of barley, and twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil”.

first.text: Kings: Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in Galilee, and “they pleased him not”.

second.text: Chronicles: “the cities which Huram had restored to Solomon, Solomon built them, and caused the children of Israel to dwell there”.
Chronicles: “four hundred and fifty talents of gold”.

questions.question: Was David's Hiram the same king as Solomon's?

views.label: A different, earlier Hiram
views.holders: Thenius and Ewald, as reported by Keil (1866)

argument.text: Josephus's Tyrian figures seem to start Hiram's reign late in David's life, so Thenius suggested that Hiram's father Abibal is meant in David's story, and Ewald that Abibal's own father was also called Hiram.

views.label: Samuel's order is by topic, not date
views.holders: Movers, as reported by Keil (1866)

argument.text: 2 Samuel 5 groups the building of Jerusalem with its capture, so Hiram's help may come years later.

views.label: Josephus's dating is his own calculation
views.holders: Keil and Delitzsch (tr. 1866)

argument.text: Keil notes that Scripture makes the same Hiram a friend of both kings, and argues that the temple-in-Hiram's-twelfth-year figure is Josephus's own reckoning, not Menander's, so Hiram may have reigned longer.

questions.question: Who gave the cities to whom: Solomon to Hiram (Kings) or Hiram to Solomon (Chronicles)?

views.label: Hiram gave back the cities he did not want
views.holders: The Geneva Bible notes (1599); the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: The Geneva note reads Chronicles as cities “which Hiram gave again to Solomon because they did not please him”; the Pulpit Commentary reads “restored” from 1 Kings 9:11, the cities having first been given to Hiram in payment.

views.label: Probably two different traditions
views.holders: W. E. Barnes, Chronicles (1899); Ellicott's Commentary

argument.text: Ellicott notes that the Hebrew says literally “which Huram gave” and calls it “a contrary transaction”; Barnes, reading “given” with the Revised Version, writes that “probably” Kings and Chronicles “follow different traditions” about these border cities, “and no reconciliation is possible”.

notSaid: Scripture does not name Hiram's father (Josephus, quoting Menander, calls him Abibalus).
Scripture gives no length of reign and does not tell how his reign ended.
No prophet in Scripture speaks to or about this Hiram; the “prince of Tyre” of Ezekiel 28 is a later king.
Scripture does not say what Hiram did with the twenty cities, beyond naming them Cabul.

places.name: Ezion-geber
places.note: Port of the Red Sea fleet

places.name: Ophir
places.note: Source of gold and almug trees

rulers.name: The queen of Sheba
otherNames: The queen of the south (Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31)
rulers.title: Queen of Sheba
rulers.tagline: She came to Solomon with hard questions.

capital.name: Sheba
capital.note: Scripture names her land, not her city or where it lay. The Atlas pin stands in south-west Arabia; where Sheba was is a question below.

identifications.text: Scripture never gives her name. “Makeda” and “Balkis” come from much later traditions; this page does not use them as her name.
Jesus calls her “the queen of the south” who “came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon”.
She is called a queen and comes and goes with her own servants; Scripture names no king beside her.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign; her visit fell in Solomon's reign.

dates.label: Placed by Solomon's reign (Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young)
dates.note: Her visit is undated. It falls within Solomon's reign, 971–932 BC in Young's table; 1 Kings tells it after the temple and the palace were finished.

scriptureSays.text: She heard “of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD”, and came to test him “with hard questions”.
“She communed with him of all that was in her heart. And Solomon told her all her questions.”
“It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thy acts and of thy wisdom. Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me.”
“Blessed be the LORD thy God, which delighted in thee, to set thee on the throne of Israel.”
“So she turned and went to her own country, she and her servants.”
Jesus: “The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it … and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here.”

claim.text: She heard “of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD”.
She came to Jerusalem “with a very great train, with camels that bare spices, and very much gold, and precious stones”.
She came “with hard questions”; “there was not any thing hid from the king, which he told her not”.
Having seen his wisdom, his house, his table, his servants and “his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD; there was no more spirit in her”.
“Because the LORD loved Israel for ever, therefore made he thee king, to do judgment and justice.”
She gave “an hundred and twenty talents of gold, and of spices very great store, and precious stones”.
Solomon gave her “all her desire, whatsoever she asked”; she returned to her own country.
Jesus set her beside the men of Nineveh as a witness against “this generation”.

worship.text: She came because of Solomon's fame “concerning the name of the LORD”.
She blessed “the LORD thy God, which delighted in thee”.

building.text: She saw “the house that he had built”, and his ascent to the house of the LORD.

alliances.text: Gifts on both sides: her gold, spices and stones; his gifts “of his royal bounty”.
1 Kings 10 places her visit amid Solomon's trade by sea and his gold; Kings records no treaty with her.

people.text: “Happy are thy men, happy are these thy servants, which stand continually before thee.”
“There came no more such abundance of spices as these which the queen of Sheba gave to king Solomon.”

claim.text: She came to Solomon in Jerusalem, tested him, and returned home.
Josephus calls her “a woman queen of Egypt and Ethiopia”, and links her with the queen Herodotus names Nicaule. He retells Kings and is not an independent witness to her.

outside.name: The Kebra Nagast (Ethiopia)
outside.date: Arabic version dated by its colophons to AD 1314–1344

claim.text: A later tradition, found in the Ethiopian Kebra Nagast (whether it is the first source was not established here), names her Makeda and gives her a son by Solomon, Menyelek, from whom Ethiopia's kings claimed descent. Its translator Budge (1922) writes that “neither of these names is ancient”.

outside.name: Arab tradition
outside.date: medieval; the first source is not established here

claim.text: Arab writers call her Balkis (Bilqis). T. H. Weir (1915) holds that the Arabs identified her with Bilqis because she was “the only Sabean queen known to them”, a queen of several centuries later.
Weir writes that the Sabaean inscriptions “do not go back far enough to throw any light upon the queen who was contemporary with Solomon”.

outside.name: Queens of Arabia in Assyrian records

claim.text: Tiglath-pileser III names two queens of Arabia who paid him tribute, Zabibe and Samsi; they lived some two centuries after Solomon and are not the queen of Sheba.

first.text: Kings: she heard “of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD”.

second.text: Chronicles: “when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon”, she came “with hard questions at Jerusalem”; it has no words about the name of the LORD.

first.text: Kings: “to set thee on the throne of Israel: because the LORD loved Israel for ever”.

second.text: Chronicles: “to set thee on his throne, to be king for the LORD thy God: because thy God loved Israel, to establish them for ever”.

first.text: Kings: all her desire, “beside that which Solomon gave her of his royal bounty”.

second.text: Chronicles: all her desire, “beside that which she had brought unto the king”.

views.label: South-west Arabia (Saba)
views.holders: W. Whiston (1737), note 16 to Antiquities 8.6.5; T. H. Weir, ISBE (1915); E. A. W. Budge (1922)

argument.text: Whiston thought it “now generally agreed” that she was a queen of Sabea in South Arabia; Weir calls Sheba a South-Arabian tribe whose capital was Marib; Budge thinks it “far more probable that her home was Shebha, or Saba, or Sheba, in the south-west of Arabia”.

views.label: Egypt and Ethiopia
views.holders: Josephus, Antiquities 8.6.5 (about AD 93)

argument.text: Josephus calls her “queen of Egypt and Ethiopia”.

views.label: Ethiopia
views.holders: The Kebra Nagast (Arabic version AD 1314–1344)

argument.text: The Ethiopian tradition makes her Makeda, queen of Ethiopia.

views.label: Scripture does not say
views.holders: 1 Kings 10; 2 Chronicles 9; Matthew 12; Luke 11

argument.text: Every passage calls her only “the queen of Sheba” or “the queen of the south”.

views.label: Makeda
views.holders: The Kebra Nagast, as reported by its translator Budge (1922)

argument.text: The Ethiopian name; Budge says it is not ancient.

views.label: Balkis (Bilqis)
views.holders: Arab writers, as reported by Budge (1922) and D. F. Roberts, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: The Arabic name; Budge says it is not ancient, and Weir that it belonged to a much later queen.

notSaid: Scripture never gives her name, her husband or family, or the length of her reign.
1 Kings 10 does not say where Sheba lay.
Scripture says nothing of a son by Solomon; that is the Kebra Nagast's tradition.
Scripture does not say what she did after she went home.

places.name: Sheba
places.note: Her land (the Atlas pin is in south-west Arabia)

rulers.name: Mesha
rulers.title: King of Moab
rulers.tagline: A sheepmaster who threw off Israel's yoke.

capital.name: Dibon
capital.note: Scripture names no capital. On his stele Mesha calls himself “the Daibonite”; the stele was found at Dibon. His last stand in 2 Kings 3 was at Kir-haraseth.

identifications.text: Mesha king of Moab (2 Kings 3:4); not Caleb's son Mesha (1 Chronicles 2:42) or the Benjamite Mesha (1 Chronicles 8:9). Kings names him once; the rest of the chapter calls him “the king of Moab”.

The Mesha of the stele, “son of Chemoshmelek, king of Moab, the Daibonite”, is taken to be this king: Driver writes that the inscription “gives particulars of the revolt of Moab from Israel, noticed briefly in 2 Ki. 1, 1 = 3, 5”.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign.

dates.label: Placed by Israel's kings (Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young)
dates.note: No year of his own is known. Kings dates his revolt after Ahab's death (853 BC on the main system) and the war against him to the reign of Jehoram of Israel (852–841 BC). Driver (1890) calls his inscription a monument of the ninth century BC.

scriptureSays.text: “Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel an hundred thousand lambs, and an hundred thousand rams, with the wool.”
“When Ahab was dead … the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.”
Besieged, “he took with him seven hundred men that drew swords, to break through even unto the king of Edom: but they could not”.

“Then he took his eldest son that should have reigned in his stead, and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall. And there was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.”

claim.text: He paid the king of Israel a hundred thousand lambs and a hundred thousand rams, “with the wool”.
“Then Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab.”
Jehoram of Israel, Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom went “the way through the wilderness of Edom”, and ran out of water.
Elisha told the kings to dig ditches: the valley would fill with water, and “he will deliver the Moabites also into your hand”.
The Moabites saw the water “as red as blood”, said the kings had “smitten one another”, ran to the spoil, and were routed.
The allies beat down the cities, covered every good piece of land with stones, stopped the wells and felled the good trees.
“Only in Kir-haraseth left they the stones thereof; howbeit the slingers went about it, and smote it.”
He tried to break through to the king of Edom with seven hundred swordsmen, “but they could not”.
He “offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall”.
“There was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.”

worship.text: He offered his eldest son as a burnt offering upon the wall of his besieged city.
On his stele he gives the glory to his god: “I made this high place for Chemosh”, and “Chemosh drave him out from before me”.

building.text: The stele lists his building: Baal-meon, Qiryathen, Aroer and “the highway by the Arnon”, Beth-Bamoth, Bezer, Medeba and Beth-Diblathen; and he says he cut “the cutting for QRHH” (a place named on the stele) “with the help of prisoner[s of] Israel”.

alliances.text: Tribute to the king of Israel in wool and flocks, until his revolt.
Against him stood Israel, Judah and Edom together.

people.text: “They gathered all that were able to put on armour, and upward, and stood in the border.”
The allies were told to “mar every good piece of land with stones”, and did so.

claim.text: Consulted by the three kings in the wilderness of Edom, he promised water and victory over Moab.

quote.text: he will deliver the Moabites also into your hand

claim.text: He paid tribute to Israel, rebelled when Ahab died, and was attacked by Jehoram.
Jehoshaphat answered Jehoram: “I will go up: I am as thou art”.
The king of Edom marched with them; Mesha tried to break through on his side.

outside.name: The Mesha Stele (the Moabite Stone)
outside.date: Ninth century BC; found at Dibon on 19 August 1868

claim.text: An inscribed stone, 3 feet 10 inches high, found at Dibon in 1868 by the missionary V. Klein, broken with fire and cold water in 1869, and largely recovered by Clermont-Ganneau; the fragments are in the Louvre.
“I am Mesha‘ son of Chemoshmelek, king of Moab, the Daibonite. My father reigned over Moab for 30 years, and I reigned after my father.”

outside.name: Mesha Stele: Omri and his son

claim.text: “Omri was king over Israel, and he afflicted Moab for many days, because Chemosh was angry with his land. And his son succeeded him; and he also said, I will afflict Moab.” Omri took the land of Medeba, and Israel dwelt there “during his days, and half his son’s days, forty years”.

He took Ataroth, which “the king of Israel” had built; took Nebo, killing “7,000 men”, devoted it to “Ashtor-Chemosh”, and dragged “the [ves]sels of YAHWEH” before Chemosh; and took Yahaz, which the king of Israel had built and held “while he fought against me”.

first.text: 2 Kings: “Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab.”

second.text: The stele: Israel dwelt in Medeba “during his [Omri's] days, and half his son’s days, forty years”. It does not name the son.

first.text: 2 Kings: the three kings routed Moab, beat down its cities, spoiled its land and besieged Kir-haraseth.

second.text: The stele tells only of Mesha's victories over Israel, at Ataroth, Nebo and Yahaz, and says “Israel perished with an everlasting destruction”.

first.text: 2 Kings: after the sacrifice on the wall “there was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him”.

second.text: The stele has no siege, no sacrifice, and no Jehoram, Jehoshaphat or Edom; it credits Chemosh: “Chemosh drave him out from before me”.

first.text: 2 Kings: Elisha speaks for the LORD: “Thus saith the LORD, Make this valley full of ditches.”

second.text: The stele: Mesha took “the [ves]sels of YAHWEH” from Nebo and “dragged them before Chemosh”.
In line 30 Driver restores a word for sheep-breeders, “the word which is actually used of Mesha himself in 2 Ki. 3, 4”, but warns that the letters “can only be regarded as conjectural”.

questions.question: When did Moab break free: after Ahab's death (Kings) or in the middle of his reign (the stele)?

views.label: After Ahab's death
views.holders: 2 Kings 1:1 and 3:5; A. H. Sayce, ISBE (1915), p. 2072

argument.text: Sayce takes the stele's “forty” as “an indefinite period of time” and writes that “the revolt of Mesha took place after Ahab's death”.

views.label: In the middle of Ahab's reign
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1890), pp. lxxxviii–lxxxix and xciv

argument.text: Driver reads the stele's “half his son’s days” as Ahab's and concludes that the revolt took place “in the middle of Ahab's reign, not after his death (as stated, 2 Ki. 1, 1)”.

views.label: A real discrepancy in the forty years
views.holders: W. Ewing, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Ewing counts only 34 years for Omri and Ahab together, 23 if half of Ahab's reign is taken, and writes: “So great a difference cannot be explained by the use of round numbers.”

questions.question: Whose eldest son was offered on the wall (2 Kings 3:27)?

views.label: Mesha's own heir
views.holders: Josephus, Antiquities 9.3.2 (about AD 93); C. F. Keil (tr. 1872), p. 307; John Gill; J. R. Lumby (1887)

argument.text: Josephus: “he took his eldest son, who was to reign after him”. Keil: “his first-born son, who was to succeed him as king”; Lumby: “his own eldest son, not as has been explained by some, the eldest son of the Edomite king”.

views.label: The king of Edom's son
views.holders: Joseph Kimchi; Moses Kimchi and Gersonides; as reported (and rejected) by John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Gill reports that Joseph Kimchi thought Mesha already held the Edomite king's son, and that Moses Kimchi and Gersonides thought he captured him in the sally, reading Amos 2:1, where Moab “burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime”.

questions.question: To whom was the sacrifice offered?

views.label: To Chemosh
views.holders: C. F. Keil (tr. 1872), p. 307; J. R. Lumby (1887); the Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott's Commentary

argument.text: Keil: “not to the God of Israel … but to his own god Camos”; Lumby and the Pulpit Commentary also name Chemosh, and Ellicott compares the stele's “Chemosh was angry with his land”.

views.label: To God
views.holders: Josephus, Antiquities 9.3.2; Ephrem the Syrian, as reported by Keil (tr. 1872), p. 307

argument.text: Josephus writes that he “offered him as a whole burnt-offering to God”; Keil names Josephus and Ephrem as holding that it was offered to the God of Israel.

questions.question: Whose “great indignation against Israel” ended the siege (2 Kings 3:27)?

argument.text: Keil holds that the phrase always means divine wrath: the human sacrifice the siege had driven Mesha to “brought a severe judgment from God upon Israel”.

views.label: The wrath of Chemosh, as Moab saw it
views.holders: Ellicott's Commentary

argument.text: Ellicott sees the phrase as a visitation of wrath, apparently a Moabite sortie, and “as the present writer understands the words”, the wrath of Chemosh falling upon the Hebrew alliance.

views.label: Human anger
views.holders: J. R. Lumby (1887); the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Lumby takes it as “wrath of men”, perhaps of Judah and Edom at having been drawn into such a sacrifice; the Pulpit Commentary also holds it “must have been human”, and thinks it was the Moabites' fury.

notSaid: Scripture does not name Mesha's father, his capital or his god; Chemosh, Dibon and his father's name come from the stele.
Scripture gives no length of reign and does not tell what became of Mesha after Israel withdrew.
Isaiah 15–16 and Jeremiah 48, the oracles on Moab, do not name him.
The stele says nothing of the campaign of 2 Kings 3, and 2 Kings says nothing of the stele's wars at Ataroth, Nebo and Yahaz.

rulers.name: Candace
rulers.title: Queen of the Ethiopians
rulers.tagline: Her treasurer met Philip on the road to Gaza.

capital.name: Ethiopia
capital.note: Acts says only “the Ethiopians”. Pliny puts a queen Candace at Meroë, and Strabo puts Candace's royal seat at Napata, both on the Nile south of Egypt; the Atlas pin for Ethiopia is near Meroë.

identifications.text: Scripture names her once, to say whose treasurer the eunuch was. Whether “Candace” was her own name or a title is a question below.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length of reign and no date.

dates.label: Scripture
dates.note: No year is given. Acts tells the story after Stephen's death and the scattering of the church from Jerusalem (Acts 8:1–5). Which queen reigned then is not known from the sources used here.

scriptureSays.text: Philip met “a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship”.
She does not appear in the story herself; Acts names her only to say whose officer he was.

claim.text: He “had come to Jerusalem for to worship”.

events.label: Reading Isaiah on the Gaza road

claim.text: Returning in his chariot he read “Esaias the prophet”; Philip asked, “Understandest thou what thou readest?”
Philip “preached unto him Jesus”; they went down into the water, “and he baptized him”.
“He went on his way rejoicing.”

worship.text: Her treasurer had come to Jerusalem to worship, and was reading the book of Isaiah.

people.text: He “had the charge of all her treasure”.

outside.name: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 6.35
outside.date: about AD 77, reporting explorers sent by Nero

claim.text: Nero's explorers reported that at Meroë “a female, whose name was Candace, ruled over the district, that name having passed from queen to queen for many years”.

outside.name: Strabo, Geography 17.1.54
outside.date: Strabo writes of a queen “in our time”, in Augustus's reign

claim.text: Strabo tells of the generals of “Candace, queen of the Ethiopians in our time, a masculine woman, and who had lost an eye”, at war with the Roman commander Petronius; Napata “was the royal seat of Candace”. This is an earlier queen than the one in Acts.
Irenaeus reports that the eunuch “was also sent into the regions of Ethiopia, to preach what he had himself believed”.

Eusebius writes that “Ethiopia even to the present day is ruled, according to ancestral custom, by a woman”, and that the eunuch “is said to have been the first on returning to his country to proclaim the knowledge of the God of the universe”.

questions.question: Was “Candace” her name or a title?

views.label: A title borne by a line of queens
views.holders: Pliny, Natural History 6.35 (about AD 77); ISBE (1915), “Candace”

argument.text: Pliny reports that the name had “passed from queen to queen for many years”; the ISBE (1915) follows him: the name had “already been borne for many years by the queens of Ethiopia”.

views.label: Acts uses it as a name
views.holders: Our reading of Acts 8:27

argument.text: Acts writes “Candace queen of the Ethiopians”, as one would a name with a title, and gives no other name.

notSaid: Scripture does not give her own name, if “Candace” is a title, nor her dates.
Scripture does not say whether she heard of her treasurer's baptism.
Acts does not say where in “Ethiopia” she reigned; Meroë and Napata come from Pliny and Strabo.
What the eunuch did on returning home is not in Scripture; Irenaeus and Eusebius report it, Eusebius with “is said”.
